nameStory: The Straight-lined Plagodis gets its name from the distinctive straight lines that run across its wings, making it easy to distinguish from other moths with wavy or curved wing patterns. It's also called the 'scorched wing' because the brownish markings on its wings can look like scorch marks from a tiny campfire.
description: This is a medium-sized moth with wings that span about 1 to 1.5 inches across when fully spread. The Straight-lined Plagodis belongs to the geometer moth family, known for their caterpillars that 'measure' the earth by looping their bodies as they crawl. The adult moths have pale yellowish to brownish wings marked with those telltale straight dark lines that give them their name. You'll spot these gentle flutterers from spring through late summer around deciduous trees.

idTips.label: Straight wing lines
idTips.description: Look for distinct, nearly perfectly straight dark lines running across both forewings - these lines don't curve or zigzag like on many other moths

idTips.label: Wing color
idTips.description: Wings are typically pale yellow, buff, or light brown with a soft, powdery texture when viewed up close

idTips.label: Wing span size
idTips.description: Wings span about the width of a large coin when spread - roughly 1 to 1.5 inches across

idTips.label: Body appearance
idTips.description: The body is slender and matches the wing color, feeling delicate and lightweight if gently handled

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat weak, fluttering motion rather than strong, direct flight

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings horizontally outward from the body rather than folded back like a butterfly

habitat: You'll find Straight-lined Plagodis moths in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially where their host trees grow. Look for them in areas with alder, birch, basswood, cherry trees, and willows - from stream valleys to forest edges and suburban areas with mature trees. They're comfortable from sea level up into the mountains wherever their favorite trees thrive.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April and May, when you might spot them fluttering around tree blossoms in the evening or find them resting on tree bark during the day.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time continues through summer months, with moths most active at dusk and drawn to porch lights and outdoor lighting.
seasonality.fall: Flight season typically ends by August, though stragglers may appear into early September in warmer years.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they overwinter in an earlier life stage, likely as eggs or pupae hidden in tree bark crevices.

funFact: The caterpillars of this moth are 'inchworms' that move by arching their backs into perfect loops - they're actually measuring your garden one tiny 'inch' at a time, and this looping locomotion is so precise that some species were historically used as living rulers by naturalists!
confusionNotes: The straight wing lines make this moth fairly distinctive, but it could be confused with other pale geometer moths. The key memory trick: if the lines across the wings look like they were drawn with a ruler rather than freehand, you've likely found a Straight-lined Plagodis.
contextualKnowledge: Geometer moths get their scientific family name from Greek words meaning 'earth measurer,' referring to how their caterpillars appear to measure distances as they loop along. The genus name Plagodis comes from Greek meaning 'oblique' or 'slanting,' though ironically this particular species is known for its straight lines rather than slanted ones.
compareHints: Since this is the only Plagodis species commonly found in New England, compare it with other pale geometer moths in the region. Unlike many of its geometer relatives that have wavy, scalloped, or zigzag wing patterns, the Straight-lined Plagodis stands out with its remarkably straight, ruler-like wing markings. Other similar-sized pale moths in the family typically have more complex or curved wing patterns.
